item.title: U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln Returns Home After Long and Grueling Deployment
item.description:
The aircraft carrier U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln, whose crew endured food shortages and mental health struggles prompted by a near-record 322-day deployment in support of the Iran war, returned on Thursday to its home port of San Diego.

Friends and family members of the crew gathered on the pier to greet the ship. They had come with signs and banners, toting American flags, and were clad in red, white and blue.

Many arrived before dawn, then erupted in thunderous cheers as the hulking vessel entered San Diego Bay with sailors in white summer uniforms manning the rails — and again when the ship docked shortly after 3 p.m. Eastern.

Family members expressed relief at the sight of their loved ones returning home after such a long and grueling assignment.

“It was nerve-racking when he went days and weeks without communication,” said Lashonda Jones, whose 20-year-old son, Jaysean Jones, is a boatswain’s mate, responsible for maintaining the ship. She sent him Bible scriptures and motivational text messages to keep his spirits high.

By longstanding Navy tradition, sailors whose spouses gave birth during the deployment were expected to be among the first to step off to meet their sons and daughters. That included 21-year-old Eduardo Morales, whose 5-month-old son Emmanuelle was on the pier early Thursday with Mr. Morales’s wife, Legna Morales.

“It’s been really hard going through labor by myself,” said Ms. Morales. “Being far away for so long, and not being there with us, not knowing the baby yet — he cries.”

The deployment for the Lincoln’s 5,000-member crew began before the war, when it left San Diego on Nov. 21, 2025. It spent almost a month at sea before pulling into the naval base in Guam for a brief stop for supplies.

The Lincoln nearly broke the record for longest carrier deployment since the Vietnam War.

The Gerald R. Ford set that record with a 327-day deployment. But unlike the Lincoln’s, the Ford’s crew was able to disembark in ports across the Mediterranean and Caribbean before steaming to the Arabian Sea before the start of the war.

The Lincoln and other ships began experiencing logistical problems after Iran destroyed the Navy’s main Middle Eastern hub in Manama, Bahrain, in response to the United States and Israel launching the war on Feb. 28.

With Iran’s ballistic missiles able to hold all ports around the Arabian Peninsula at risk of attack, the Navy’s warships in the region began to experience shortages of food, fuel and other goods as the service moved its supply hub to the British-owned island of Diego Garcia about 2,200 miles away.

The first indications of problems came from family members of Lincoln sailors, who sent reporters photos of meager meals served on the ship while supplies were running low. Many families tried to send their loved ones care packages to make up the difference, only to have their mail lost, destroyed or delivered months late.

The reports rankled Navy leaders, who downplayed the problems.

In a social media post in August, the Navy’s acting secretary, Hung Cao, accused reporters of presenting Lincoln’s sailors as “victims.” Six days later, the carrier left the Arabian Sea to begin its journey home after another carrier, the Japan-based U.S.S. George Washington, took its place.

The next month, in response to questions from Democratic lawmakers, Mr. Cao acknowledged that eight sailors from the Lincoln strike group had tried to take their own lives. One jumped overboard, and another tried to do so before being stopped by shipmates.

When asked in August about the reported problems aboard the Lincoln, Mr. Trump dismissed the concerns raised by the families of crew members. When pressed about whether he was worried about the crew’s mental health and whether he thought the deployment had gone on too long, the president said, “No. No. No.” He added that the deployment — then more than eight months long — had not been “nearly long enough.”

Some family members gathered on the pier Thursday said the challenges aboard the ship were real — including the rationing of food.

“It was pathetic,” Victoria Tozzi, whose son enlisted after high school to help fund his college education, said of the portions of food. “It looked gross, and he was like, ‘yeah it’s pretty bad.’”

When she learned that Iran had launched attacks at the ship, and that the missiles and drones had been intercepted, she asked how he was doing.

“He said, ‘Everybody is just on edge,’” she said.

Speaking to reporters Thursday after arriving back to San Diego, the Lincoln’s commanding officer, Capt. Daniel J. Keeler, said that the crew faced some challenges soon after combat operations began.

“But I had enough food. I had all the supplies I needed to conduct combat,” he added. “We never missed a mission. I also never missed a meal. We served four meals a day — 14,000 to 16,000 a day to the entire crew.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who flew to the Lincoln from San Diego on Wednesday to ride the ship for its final stretch, acknowledged the lengthy deployment in remarks to the crew on Wednesday. But he criticized reports of logistics problems as overblown. He also awarded the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest decoration that can be given to a unit of the Navy or Marine Corps for valorous service.

“There were a few folks in the media who tried to turn the U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln into some sort of a symbol — a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission,” Mr. Hegseth said, speaking into a microphone before a crowd of sailors. “And what I look out at right here and when I talk to your leadership — and I’ve had a chance to talk to a number of you — I know it is the exact opposite.”

The war with Iran has placed the Navy’s fleet of 11 nuclear-powered aircraft carriers under tremendous strain. Two carriers, the John C. Stennis and Harry S. Truman, are unavailable because of the refueling of their nuclear reactors. Another five have already played a role during the war. In July, the Ford entered a shipyard for long-delayed maintenance, and the 50-year-old Nimitz is scheduled to be decommissioned next year.

That leaves only the Dwight D. Eisenhower, the Carl Vinson and the Ronald Reagan as potentially available to deploy should the war, which is now in its eighth month, continue.

The pace of operations for the Lincoln and its crew during their extended deployment was unrelenting, as the ship played a major role in the air campaign over Iran. In August, a Navy official said that the ship launched more than 10,000 sorties and dropped more than 1.5 million pounds of ordnance during the conflict.

Aircraft aboard the Lincoln also played a key part in enforcing Mr. Trump’s blockade of Iranian ports.

In early May, an F/A-18 Super Hornet launched from the Lincoln fired its 20-millimeter cannon at the rudders of an Iranian-flagged tanker, the M/T Hasna, disabling the ship as it attempted to pass through the blockade line. A month later, another Super Hornet from the Lincoln fired a precision-guided munition into the engineering spaces aboard the Palau-flagged tanker M/T Marivex in the Gulf of Oman as it steamed toward Iran. The ship’s 24 crew members were rescued by an Omani military helicopter.

In his remarks Wednesday, Mr. Hegseth said the extended deployment was worthwhile, crediting the crew with demonstrating enormous resilience.

“What makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you are resilient and you overcome,” he added. “You finish the mission nonetheless. Yes, it’s hard. That’s why you’re here, and you do difficult and hard things. But you believe in your heart in that mission.”

“My heart only swells with pride just standing in front of all of you,” he added.

On the pier Thursday, the same sentiment rippled through the crowd of friends and family, which included Jason Tisdale, a retired master chief gunner’s mate.

“My son,” Mr. Tisdale said, pausing to choke back tears, “makes me very proud. Having him back here is great. I’m glad him and the rest of the crew are home safe. It was tough out there. A tough deployment — very long — but now we’re on the other side of it.”

He added: “I’m very happy, and we just want to welcome him back with open arms and tell him we love him.”

In all, the Lincoln’s crew spent nearly nine and a half months at sea without a break until the Lincoln pulled in to Pattaya, Thailand, on Sept. 2 for five days of rest.

On Sept. 18, the Lincoln reached U.S. soil during a brief stop in Guam. The crew was allowed to get off the ship so long as they stayed on the naval base there.

Now, back on the mainland, the crew will get a bit more time off.

When a warship returns from a lengthy deployment, about half the crew typically takes two weeks of leave. The other half maintains a Monday-to-Friday workweek, but can then go home. After those two weeks are up, the groups swap, and the other half goes on leave.

item.title: Microsoft Is Suspended From Green Card Program as Trump Officials Widen Fraud Drive
item.description:
Vice President JD Vance announced on Thursday that Microsoft would be suspended from using a visa program that allowed foreign workers to permanently reside in the United States after an investigation found that the tech giant had “abused” the system.

Mr. Vance made the announcement in a news conference where he and other Trump administration officials made a slew of allegations that American companies and universities were committing visa fraud. Microsoft, they announced, is just the largest of several technology companies to face such a suspension, and schools including Harvard and Yale are now under investigation.

Mr. Vance took aim at the embattled H-1B visa program, which allows companies to hire skilled foreign workers in hard-to-fill jobs. The Trump administration has sought to overhaul the program, including imposing fees for the visas, claiming that it has unfairly allowed companies to sideline Americans and hire foreign workers. Mr. Vance has called the program “broken” and said he would support eliminating it.

Mr. Vance said on Thursday that companies like Microsoft had been using the H-1B visa program to exploit the Labor Department’s permanent labor certification program, known as PERM, which allows H-1B visa recipients to obtain a green card and potentially stay in the United States indefinitely.

Officials said that other companies suspended from PERM would include Adobe and several large information technology outsourcing firms. Mr. Vance said the suspension would “last as long as it needs to.”

The announcement on Thursday, which included officials from several agencies, was the latest attempt by the administration to seize on purported fraud to argue that exploitation of the country’s immigration system — and not President Trump’s policies — has been depriving Americans of jobs, wages and paths to prosperity.

“The Department of Labor is taking historic action by shutting down the pipeline of systemic fraud, the fraud that has flooded our country with foreign labor at the expense of American workers,” said Keith Sonderling, the labor secretary. “It begins with universities and companies that have turned into visa mills, promoting foreign workers that have lied about their qualifications to take jobs from our beloved American workers.”

But the administration has not always provided evidence to match its fraud claims. And several of its targets on Thursday disputed its assertions.

Mr. Vance directed his harshest criticism at Microsoft, saying that there had been “no company in the United States, unfortunately, that has abused this system more.”

Mr. Vance said that in the past year, the company had laid off 6,000 American workers, while it benefited from 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards. He referred to the visa holders as “indentured servants” who were paid a fraction of what their American counterparts would be.

“In other words, if you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” Mr. Vance said. “Now that is a scandalous system that we’ve allowed in this country for far too long.”

“And so our message to Microsoft is: You’re a great American company, but you’ve got to hire great American workers,” he added. “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”

In a statement, Microsoft challenged some of Mr. Vance’s claims.

The company said the “vast majority” of its employees in the United States are citizens. It said that of the roughly 6,000 H-1B applications it made last fiscal year, 80 percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees. The remaining applications were for people already legally in the country who then joined Microsoft, the company said.

“They are not new arrivals to our country,” it added.

Microsoft said its pay is among the highest in tech and among H-1B filings.

“Microsoft succeeds as a global technology leader by developing the world’s best technology work force,” the company said. “We do this by strengthening this country’s talent pipeline, hiring American workers and attracting the best talent from around the world.”

On the academic front, Mr. Vance maintained that universities were employing foreign graduate students as research assistants at lower wages, and suggested that the visas were being overused and sucking up federal funding.

Anthony D’Esposito, the inspector general of the Labor Department, announced that the agency was launching investigations into several universities for potential abuses of the J-1 visa, a cultural exchange program that allows foreign students to work and study in the United States.

“Subpoenas have been served, investigations are underway, and nobody will be getting a free pass because their name is carved into an expensive building,” he said.

The schools under investigation are Harvard, Yale, Stanford, Arizona State, Brown, M.I.T., the University of Pittsburgh, the University of California, Davis, and the California Institute of Technology.

Stanford said in a statement that it “complies with all applicable visa laws, including those relating to J-1 visas,” and “will cooperate with the investigation.”

Brian Clark, a spokesman for Brown University, said in a statement that the university had received the subpoena “for various records pertaining to foreign labor programs administered by the U.S. government, and we will respond promptly and directly.”

“Brown’s international scholars, students and employees make essential contributions on our campus, including to teaching and research that advances American innovation, competitiveness and economic vitality,” Mr. Clark said.

Arizona State University, noting that it educates more science, technology, engineering and math majors than any other university and employs one of the largest technical and scientific workforces in the country, said that it “has hired the talent needed to perform these functions and done so in complete compliance with existing United States policy and law.”

The H-1B program has long been the target of bipartisan calls for changes, but has become a centerpiece of Mr. Trump’s immigration crackdown agenda. Economists have maintained that the visa holders boost American productivity and raise wages even for American workers.

Mr. Vance, pressed on how the use of the certification program amounted to fraud, said that companies were misrepresenting that they were bringing in workers with “hyper-specialized and hyper-capable” skill sets.

Mr. Vance said that there was a difference between bringing in foreign workers like the tech tycoon Elon Musk, “who wants to come in and build something great in the United States of America,” versus an accountant at a lower wage.

“You’re not bringing in a genius to build a great American corporation,” Mr. Vance said. “You are committing fraud against the American people and against this visa program.”

Hours after the announcement, President Trump awarded Satya Nadella, Microsoft’s chief executive, the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at a summit in Washington where Mr. Musk and other tech executives also were honored.

Mr. Nadella came to the United States for graduate school and joined Microsoft in 1992. Two years later, he wrote in his memoir, he turned in his permanent residency for an H-1B visa so that his wife could immediately join him in the United States. (At the time, he said, the spouses of green card holders faced a long wait for visa approval.) Both eventually gained citizenship, and he rose through the ranks to revive Microsoft from a yearslong slump. It is now worth almost $4 trillion.

In awarding Mr. Nadella the highest honor in technology on Thursday, Mr. Trump said it was “so well deserved,” and that Mr. Nadella had turned Microsoft into “an early leader in superintelligence.”

Karen Weise contributed reporting from Seattle, Alan Blinder from Atlanta, Vimal Patel from Denver and Mark Arsenault from Boston.

item.title: The Seashells Case Against Comey at a Crossroads
item.description:
James Comey is accused of sending a coded threat to murder President Trump by posting an image of seashells on Instagram. The case against him is nearing a crucial turning point.

Comey, the former F.B.I. director fired by Trump in his first term, was indicted in April for posting a photograph of seashells arranged to form the number 8647. The Justice Department contended that “86” means “kill.” Everyone agrees that “47” refers to Trump. The four digits together, prosecutors said, amounted to a threat to kill the president.

Comey’s lawyers have asked the judge to dismiss the indictment in motions that “are now ripe for decision,” Judge Louise Wood Flanagan wrote late last month. Unless she grants one of them, the case will go to trial next year.

Judge Flanagan, who was appointed by President George W. Bush, has been hard to read. She has not scheduled oral arguments on the motions and may rule based only on the written briefs. In June, moreover, she said she would not accept friend-of-the court briefs.

That seemed odd to me, as the case presents serious free-speech issues with implications beyond the particular dispute. But some law professors who had hoped to submit briefs told me that the judge may have made a defensible choice to avoid a flood of distracting and duplicative filings.

First Amendment scholars have written that the government’s allegations about Comey’s seashell threat is problematic as a matter of language, precedent and common sense. The most common dictionary definitions of “86,” for starters, are to throw out, eject, get rid of or refuse service to.

Comey’s lawyers said that there is a fundamental problem at the heart of the case: The image of the seashells, they say, cannot amount to a threat.

In response, the government’s main argument was that a jury, rather than Judge Flanagan, should decide whether the image conveyed a true threat. A cynic might think that the administration was more interested in prolonging the prosecution than in resolving the legal questions since it will take much longer to have a jury to weigh in than letting Judge Flanagan rule.

The briefs clarified one commonly misunderstood point. The case is not about whether the seashells sought to incite violence against Trump by others. The government’s brief gestured in that direction in passing, but the laws Comey is charged with violating and the relevant precedents require something else.

The question for Judge Flanagan is whether an objective observer would understand the image of the seashells to be a serious expression of Comey’s own intent to kill the president. Only such a message would amount to a “true threat,” which is a category of speech unprotected by the First Amendment and the basis for the charges against him.

The Supreme Court has said that speech much more direct than seashell formations did not qualify as a true threat.

In 1969, it threw out a case against a draft protester charged with threatening President Lyndon B. Johnson. “If they ever make me carry a rifle,” the protester said, “the first man I want to get in my sights is L.B.J.”

The court ruled that the remark was “political hyperbole” and not a true threat because it was conditional, made at a rally and greeted by laughter.

Prosecutors could have charged Comey with inciting others to commit violence — but they did not. Incitement, like a true threat, is not protected by the First Amendment. But the Supreme Court has defined incitement quite narrowly. The message at issue, the court has said, must be both intended to produce imminent violence or lawlessness and also likely to do so.

In 1969, in Brandenburg v. Ohio, the Supreme Court unanimously overturned the conviction of a leader of a Ku Klux Klan group under an Ohio statute that banned the advocacy of terrorism. The Klan leader, Clarence Brandenburg, had urged his followers at a rally to “send the Jews back to Israel” and to “bury” Black people, using a racial slur.

Because Brandenburg’s words fell short of calling for immediate violence in a setting where such violence was likely, the Supreme Court ruled that he could not be prosecuted for incitement.

Trump has been the beneficiary of that ruling. When he was running for president in 2016, he pointed to some protesters at one of his rallies and told the crowd to “get ’em out of here.”

The protesters, who said they were then viciously assaulted by others in the crowd, sued Trump for inciting a riot. Trump won the suit. A federal appeals court, referring to Brandenburg, ruled that his exhortation was protected by the First Amendment.

In the Comey case, prosecutors said they would demonstrate to the jury that “86” was “a term of art in the context of organized crime.”

John Gleeson, a former federal judge and mafia prosecutor, submitted a sworn statement debunking that idea based on his many hundreds of hours of listening to the surreptitiously recorded conversations of gangsters and to the accounts of cooperating witnesses.

He made clear that he was not submitting the statement as a professional courtesy to a fellow former prosecutor. He and Comey had butted heads while serving in different U.S. attorney’s office in New York City, he said. “Mr. Comey and I are not friends and never were,” Gleeson wrote.

Got a news tip about the courts? If you have information to share about the Supreme Court or other federal courts, please contact us.

But Gleeson scoffed at the government’s theory. A mobster might “whack” or “clip” someone, he wrote.

But “the claim that ’86’ is mafia jargon for ‘kill’ is preposterous,” Gleeson wrote. “If it weren’t made in the context of seeking to deprive a man of his liberty, it would be laughable.”

A couple of weeks ago, I wrote about the 11th Circuit’s puzzling postponements of arguments over the release of a report from Jack Smith, the special counsel who tried to prosecute Trump on charges that he had mishandled classified documents. The appeals court first scheduled the arguments for June 2026 and then repeatedly postponed them, tentatively settling on the week of Jan. 18, 2027.

Last week, the court had a change of heart, setting the case down for argument on Nov. 2. As night follows day, a lawyer for Trump on Monday asked the appeals court to put the argument off again — asking that it once again be pushed into next year.

“Given President Trump’s extensive commitments, including travel and other obligations in advance of the Nov. 3, 2026, federal midterm elections, counsel will not have sufficient opportunity to meaningfully confer with her client,” the lawyer, Kendra Wharton, wrote.

In a response filed Tuesday, two watchdog groups seeking the report — the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University and American Oversight — urged the appeals court to get on with it.

“Time is of the essence in this appeal,” they wrote. “Appellants seek public access to a document of singular historic importance — one that concerns the character of the nation’s highest elected official.”

Judge James Ho of the Fifth Circuit, a Trump appointee often mentioned as a potential Supreme Court nominee and sometimes accused of angling for a promotion, used a concurring opinion in a minor case that tangentially involved criticism of a magistrate judge to muse about the impossibility of refuting the accusation that he is auditioning. “No one has the power to look into another man’s heart and ascertain his actual motivations or ambitions,” he wrote. “So the accusation of auditioning is indeed irrefutable. Certain actions may seem like auditioning to some, but to others, it’s simply doing the job as the judge best sees fit.”

A federal judge in Florida dismissed criminal charges against a noncitizen who was accused of voting in a federal election in 2020, ruling that Congress had been powerless to enact the 1996 law requiring voters to be citizens under which she was prosecuted. It’s not as crazy as it sounds. For starters, the judge, David Leibowitz, had appointed Paul Clement, a former solicitor general, to explore the question as a friend of the court. Clement and a colleague, Chadwick Harper, concluded that the law was “likely unconstitutional.”

Jack Goldsmith, a law professor at Harvard and a former Justice Department official in the Bush administration, assessed Justice Samuel Alito’s new book, “So Ordered,” in The Atlantic. “His results-focused jurisprudence, his culture-warrior profile, and his scorn for fainthearted conservative jurists mesh with the Trump-inspired movement,” Goldsmith wrote of Alito.

Mailbag

How exactly is the 25th Amendment invoked? — Sheila Boyd

The 25th Amendment, which was adopted in 1967, includes a provision setting out an elaborate method of removing the president.It has never been tested.

The process contemplated by the provision starts when the vice president and a majority of the cabinet notify Congress that “the president is unable to discharge the powers and duties of his office.” Once that happens, “the vice president shall immediately assume the powers and duties of the office as acting president.”

But that may only be the beginning of the process. Should the ousted president object, removal requires a two-thirds vote of both the House and the Senate. That is a tougher requirement than removal by impeachment, which requires a majority in the House and a two-thirds vote of the Senate.

I would love to hear your questions on the law, the courts or whatever is on your mind. Send them my way at the-docket@nytimes.com.

Closing Argument

Justice Alito rejected speculation that he might step down if Democrats retake the Senate in next month’s election. A retirement in November, should the Democrats win, would allow Trump to name his successor while Republicans remain in control in the lame-duck session.

“I intend to stick around through this term,” he told Greg Stohr of Bloomberg News in an interview conducted last week and published Tuesday. “I made that decision many months ago.”

The Supreme Court’s term started Monday and will run through late June or early July.

In an interview with Jan Crawford of CBS News, Justice Alito, who is 76, said that retirement is “something I think that somebody at my age has to think about every term.”

Those interviews and several other recent ones were part of the justice’s efforts to promote his new book, and they mostly covered familiar territory. But one surprise in the interview with CBS News concerned Obergefell v. Hodges, the 2015 decision establishing a constitutional right to same-sex marriage. He indicated that it is not in peril.

Justice Alito dissented in the case and later indicated that it ought to be reconsidered. But his 2022 majority opinion in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization took pains to say that eliminating the constitutional right to abortion the court was not putting Obergefell at risk even though it shared a methodology with Roe v. Wade.

He went even further in the interview.

“I did not think that there was any realistic prospect that it would be overruled because of the passage of time and the developments in the country,” he explained to Crawford.

“One of the important factors we take into account in deciding whether we should re-examine a past decision is the degree to which there has been reliance on the decision,” he added. It would certainly seem that the many couples who built their lives around marriages that they were only able to enter into as a result of the ruling relied on it.

Justice Anthony Kennedy, who wrote the majority opinion in Obergefell and retired in 2018, made this point when I interviewed him last year.

“A powerful argument against” overruling the decision, he said, was the “tremendous amount of reliance” that same-sex couples and their families had placed on the decision.

Please send me your comments on seashells, the 25th Amendment, lame-duck sessions or anything else at the-docket@nytimes.com. See you next week. — Adam

item.title: Security Guard Fatally Shoots Armed Man at Nashville Federal Courthouse
item.description:
A security guard shot and killed a man who was armed with a gun at an entry checkpoint in the federal courthouse building in Nashville on Thursday morning, the authorities said.

The man, who was in his 40s, tried to enter the front door of the Fred D. Thompson U.S. Courthouse and Federal Building around 9:30 a.m. local time and tried to fire his gun, “but it did not fire,” Don Aaron, a spokesman for the Metropolitan Nashville Police, told reporters at the scene.

The man then “transitioned to a knife” at the checkpoint, Mr. Aaron said, which led to a confrontation with a security guard who then shot the man.

The man, who was from out of state and whose name was not released, was critically wounded and taken to Vanderbilt University Medical Center, where he died, Mr. Aaron said.

It was not clear why the man was at the courthouse. Rob McGuire, first assistant U.S. attorney for the Middle District of Tennessee, said in an interview that the man was not listed as a defendant or plaintiff in court records.

The authorities searched the man’s vehicle, which was parked outside the building, and “found nothing threatening inside the car,” Mr. Aaron said.

A spokeswoman for the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said in a statement that the department was assisting in the investigation.

Other agencies including the F.B.I., the U.S. Marshals Service and the Nashville police were also assisting with the investigation, Mr. McGuire said.

Local TV outlets showed a large police presence near the courthouse. Mr. Aaron said the nearby Nashville Public Library had been evacuated “out of an abundance of caution.”

Mr. McGuire said that the front entrance to the building was closed on Thursday and that most employees sheltered in place during the shooting, which took place during a busy time at the courthouse. Prosecutors, judges and members of Mr. McGuire’s staff work in the building, which also has offices for Senators Marsha Blackburn and Bill Hagerty of Tennessee.

“We are thankful it was not worse,” Mr. McGuire said, noting that this was the first time this type of episode happened at the courthouse, which opened in 2022.

item.title: Trump Administration Asks Supreme Court to Weigh In, Again, in TV Ad Fight
item.description:
The Trump administration filed an emergency application to the Supreme Court on Thursday asking the justices to intervene, once again, in an ongoing fight over whether political parties are entitled to the same low-cost TV ad rates as candidates in the midterms.

The dispute deals with an obscure but critical part of the rules surrounding political advertising, on who can qualify for low-cost ad rates. Democrats have had an advantage in that area in recent years. With hotly contested elections looming, Democrats and Republicans have been fighting the issue through the courts.

Democrats have been thought to benefit from the old rules, which limited low rates to candidates because they tended to raise more money than their party’s committees. The opposite is true for Republicans.

Last month, the justices handed Republicans a victory, concluding that, at least for now, political parties and joint fund-raising committees were entitled to the same low-cost TV ad rates as candidates have long received.

The new emergency application was prompted by an appeals court decision on Wednesday against the administration on the issue. Solicitor General D. John Sauer urged the justices to overturn that ruling, calling it “a flagrant abuse” of the judiciary’s power to order a federal agency to take action and “a baseless effort to circumvent a prior” decision by the justices.

Shortly after Mr. Sauer filed his application, Republican groups similarly asked the justices to weigh in.

Under the 1971 Federal Election Campaign Act, which sets out regulations for how TV stations must interact with political candidates during election seasons, broadcasters are required, in the weeks before an election, to give political candidates low rates to buy TV ad time — a key way to reach voters.

Republicans have long claimed other political entities should also have access to the lower rates. The current tangled battle over the issue began in March, when the F.C.C. announced that broadcasters would be required for the first time to extend low-cost ad rates to political parties engaged in coordinated expenditures with candidates, as well as to joint fund-raising committees with political-party members.

Four Democratic candidates in key battlegrounds — Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, former Senator Sherrod Brown of Ohio, former Gov. Roy Cooper of North Carolina and Representative Kristen McDonald Rivet of Michigan — objected and sued.

In August, a three-judge panel from the Fourth Circuit sided with the Democratic candidates.

National Republican groups then appealed to the Supreme Court and won in early September, allowing party committees to receive the lower ad rates as the lower court litigation continued.

As the case moved through the courts, the F.C.C. had yet to wrap up its review of the new policy. The candidates accuse the agency of purposely stalling in formalizing the ad scheme, potentially in an effort to forestall any court rulings against it before the November vote.

Yesterday, in a divided ruling, a three-judge panel on the Fourth Circuit agreed and ordered the F.C.C. to finalize its rules by noon on Friday.

Judges Robert B. King, a Clinton appointee, joined by James A. Wynn, an Obama appointee, wrote that the federal agency was “dragging its feet.” The court had “accorded the F.C.C. a substantial amount of grace, but its gamesmanship must end,” Judge King added.

item.title: Trump Administration Considers Using Ships to Deport Immigrants
item.description:
The Trump administration is considering using ships, including a 500-foot training vessel and ferries, to deport migrants to Central and South America on journeys that could take days and cost millions of dollars, according to two U.S. officials.

The discussions over recent weeks are still preliminary, but officials have identified possible ships, including the Training Ship Golden Bear, a maritime academy vessel docked in California, said one person who spoke on the condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the plan. Defense Department officials have also reached out to companies about ships in Europe, the official said.

A different official, from the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees deportations, cautioned that the plan was still hypothetical and that no decisions had been made.

It is not clear why officials are entertaining such an unusual plan, considering the logistical challenges, high cost and checkered history of deportations by sea. The plan could, however, offload some deportation costs from Homeland Security to the Defense Department.

“D.H.S. is assessing all our resources, to maximize efficiency and continue to deliver on President Trump’s mission of securing the homeland for all Americans,” the Homeland Security Department said in a statement. Secretary Markwayne Mullin, the statement added, “is 100 percent focused on ensuring the needs of our department are met while being the best possible steward of taxpayer dollars.”

What you should know about anonymous sources. The Times makes a careful decision any time it shields the identity of a source. The information the source supplies must be newsworthy, credible and give readers genuine insight.

The Defense Department did not comment on the proposal.

The plan would represent another escalation of the Trump administration’s evolving strategy for carrying out mass deportations using all available means. Those drastic steps have included flying people abroad using military planes, sending migrants to unfamiliar and often dangerous third countries, and housing people in Guantánamo Bay, Cuba. The administration has also embraced policies to deter immigrants from coming to the United States and persuade them to self-deport.

“What ICE is functionally contemplating is prison ships,” said Claire Trickler-McNulty, a former top official at Immigration and Customs Enforcement during the Biden administration. “That raises serious concerns at every step. Moving people through international waters and past other countries’ territory for days at a time raises hard questions about which laws apply and who has jurisdiction if something goes wrong.”

She added that “holding hundreds of people on a ship is also an enormous operational and safety challenge.”

Ms. Trickler-McNulty said that during her time at the Homeland Security Department, including as a career official in the Obama and first Trump administrations, agency staff considered various ideas to deport people, such as using ships or trains. But they never pursued them seriously, she said.

The journeys to countries like El Salvador, Honduras and Venezuela would take days by sea and require a large number of security personnel. It is unclear whether migrants would be detained for the duration of the trips or what their sleeping arrangements would be.

The U.S. government has estimated that using ships could cost millions of dollars per trip, whereas deportation flights are substantially cheaper. It is also unclear whether other countries would agree to such a plan.

The Golden Bear served as a training ship for the Cal Poly Maritime Academy, a school for those seeking careers at sea, as a key part of the school’s educational program. The vessel ended its 30-year run with the school this summer. It is not clear under what authority the ship could be used for deportations by the federal government.

“For three decades, Golden Bear has served as a floating classroom where thousands of cadets transformed classroom knowledge into practical experience at sea,” a July announcement from the school read.

Such a plan would also conjure memories of a controversial 1950s campaign in which hundreds of thousands of Mexicans were deported in a large-scale deportation drive referred to as Operation Wetback. The campaign, named for a slur for Mexican immigrants, included expelling people by sea.

In August 1956, chaos erupted aboard one of the ships near the Mexican border city of Tampico. The New York Times reported that 40 passengers jumped from the ship and that five drowned.

The Mexican government had shut down the operation by September, citing poor weather. The Times reported, however, that the “prevailing opinion” was that it was because of the incident near Tampico as well as “alleged unsatisfactory facilities on ship and maltreatment of involuntary passengers.”

John Ismay and Jazmine Ulloa contributed reporting.

item.title: 5-Year-Old Dies After Digital Whiteboard Falls in School Classroom
item.description:
A 5-year-old student at a Florida elementary school died on Wednesday after a 120-pound video display board fell on him in his classroom, the school district said.

Bellamy Dawkins-Morris was seriously injured when a digital board fell on him just after 11:30 a.m. at Riviera Elementary School in Palm Bay, about 70 miles southeast of Orlando, the Palm Bay Police Department said. School staff members called 911 and administered first aid until emergency responders arrived, law enforcement officials said, but Bellamy died after being transported to a hospital.

Brevard Public Schools, the school district, said in a statement on Thursday that the large video display had been mounted on a wall by a licensed third-party vendor in accordance with manufacturer guidelines. The board was made by Promethean, an education technology company, and the district said all of its boards made by the company were being inspected.

“The safety and well-being of our students and staff remain our highest priority,” Dr. Mark Rendell, the superintendent for Brevard Public Schools, said in the statement. “We will continue to work closely with law enforcement, take appropriate precautions to ensure the safety of our school communities, and provide additional information when it becomes available and appropriate to share.”

Promethean said in a statement that it was also investigating the incident.

Family members told the local TV news station WESH 2, an NBC affiliate, that Bellamy had been moving the display board back and forth while other students were lining up when it tipped over and fell on him. The family told the local news network that Bellamy was autistic.

“When he sees things in motion, he’s going to keep pushing it to keep it in motion; that’s just something that children on the spectrum do,” Miriam Rodriguez, Bellamy’s great-aunt, told WESH 2. “Obviously, the monitor was not secure, and that’s a huge issue. That could have been anybody’s child.”

The Palm Bay Police Department said its special victims unit was investigating the incident.

Dr. Rendell, the superintendent, said at a news conference on Wednesday that he had met with Bellamy’s family shortly after the child’s death.

“We lost a life today, a precious young life. There are no words to describe that loss,” Dr. Rendell said. “I’ve been doing this for over 30 years, and I really couldn’t find the words to share with them my grief and the grief that all of us have.”

Promethean displays are used in classrooms around the world, sometimes in lieu of traditional blackboards. The interactive panels display lesson plans and have touch-screen features.

“All of us at Promethean are heartbroken by the death of a child in the tragic accident at Riviera Elementary School,” a spokesman for Promethean said in a statement. “Nothing matters more to us than the safety of the students and teachers who use our products every day.”

item.title: Pentagon Draws Up New Iran Strike Plans as Trump Hesitates
item.description:
The U.S. military is preparing options to restart major combat operations against Iran, even as President Trump continues to show ambivalence about restarting the war, according to American officials.

Three aircraft carriers will soon be in the Middle East, a massive assembly of force, and the Pentagon, on Mr. Trump’s orders, has developed plans to strike Iran’s drone and missile arsenal, energy facilities and other military sites.

But Mr. Trump has repeatedly decided not to relaunch heavy combat operations against Iran. And the U.S. military response to Iran has been more muted in recent weeks, despite Iran’s escalating attacks on oil tankers.

In a social media post on Thursday, Mr. Trump said that he would not attack Iran before the midterm elections, and that the two countries were “having productive discussions.”

In recent months, officials said, Mr. Trump’s national security team and the Pentagon have made five proposals to him for major operations against either Iran or the Houthis, an Iranian-backed militia based in Yemen. Each time, Mr. Trump vetoed the plans.

But Mr. Trump has once more ordered up strike options. Senior national security officials, led by Vice President JD Vance, discussed plans at a meeting last Friday at Camp David. The plans center on a short, intense campaign lasting about three days, according to people briefed on the proposal.

The strikes would focus on Iran’s missile and drone arsenal, much of which Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has rebuilt since the early phase of the war. Other targets could include Iranian energy facilities and Revolutionary Guard command posts and headquarters.

The latest plans were earlier reported by Axios.

Officials have backed Mr. Trump’s assessment that some progress is being made in diplomatic talks, which have continued through mediators. The talks have continued to get hung up on the issue of Iran’s nuclear program. American officials want to reach a deal on Iran’s nuclear ambitions first, while Iranian negotiators insist that those discussions must come last.

Over the months, Iran has become a tougher opponent as its military tactics improved. Taking down Iranian missiles has required more interceptors than earlier in the war, posing challenges to America’s already taxed arsenal of munitions. Armed with satellite imagery from Chinese companies, Iran has also been able to more effectively target U.S. bases, according to people briefed on the intelligence.

Since September, the time of the last significant exchange of retaliatory attacks, Iran has struck at least 13 ships, according to a monitoring group run by the British Navy. Intelligence reports have put the number higher, at nearly 20, according to people briefed on the information. None of those attacks generated a major U.S. response.

While oil exports from the Middle East are up, Iran’s increased attacks have spooked shippers and raised questions about future energy shipments.

Throughout the summer, the U.S. military regularly retaliated after Iranian attacks on international shipping. But the far less robust response since then reflects Mr. Trump’s hesitancy to restart the war in full, officials say.

U.S. commanders are also concerned about the increasing difficulty of stopping Iranian attacks against bases where American troops are stationed, and energy facilities and other civilian infrastructure in the region.

On Thursday, in his social media post, Mr. Trump insisted that none of the oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz was coming from Iran. That is debatable, according to people briefed on intelligence reports. Iran allows some vessels to pass that have paid fees or that potentially carry some of its oil. Iran also has its own dark fleet of tankers, according to current and former officials.

Chinese companies have paid fees to Iran to transit the strait, and Iran has long secretly blended its oil with Iraqi oil to avoid sanctions. The Treasury Department on Thursday sanctioned 17 vessels that it said were part of Iran’s shadow fleet smuggling oil.

Even members of Mr. Trump’s inner circle are increasingly skeptical that military action will change Tehran’s calculus or plans. Some of these officials believe that the Trump administration’s campaign of economic pressure is working and just needs more time to force Iran to make meaningful concessions.

Even before Mr. Trump said there would be no strike before the November vote, officials had predicted that he would wait until after the Israeli elections, on Oct. 27, and the U.S. midterms the following week to decide whether to attack.

But U.S. military commanders are ready to begin larger operations in the coming days, in case the president shifts again.

The Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group left San Diego last week and will join the George H.W. Bush and the George Washington carriers as early as the end of October. Each strike group includes other warships carrying attack helicopters and Marines. It will be the first time since 2003 that three aircraft carriers will be in the Middle East.

At the end of the month, there will be more than 20,000 sailors and Marines afloat, along with hundreds of aircraft. But the high troop level will be only temporary. The George Washington is expected to return to its base in Japan soon after the Roosevelt arrives next month to replace it.

Despite the force buildup, it is hardly certain that Mr. Trump will give a green light to any new attacks even after the election. Senior U.S. officials are worried about further depleting the global arsenal of defensive weapons to defend bases in the Middle East, as well as the U.S. ability to intercept Iranian attacks.

Still other officials in favor of resumed operations note that Iran’s economy continues to weaken, and a short, intense barrage could intensify Tehran’s problems, especially if it hurts Iran’s ability to control the strait, according to current and former officials.

The United States has continued to take out Iranian drones and cruise missiles. But it has not attacked Iran’s dark tanker fleet or conducted retaliatory strikes inside Iran.

At the beginning of the war, the U.S. military in most cases fired two interceptors at incoming Iranian missiles, focusing on the most dangerous volleys.

But American officials now say Iran’s improved tactics and targeting have forced the United States and its regional partners to fire more missiles to thwart salvos aimed at American bases in the region.

American commanders say they still have reserves of interceptors as the war has drained stockpiles, and U.S. Central Command, which oversees military operations in the Middle East, has pulled in weaponry from Europe and Asia.

Reporting was contributed by Jonathan Swan and Alan Rappeport in Washington; David E. Sanger in Cambridge, Mass.; and Farnaz Fassihi in New York.

item.title: 21 Birds Are Found at Miami Airport Stuffed in Underwear and Hidden in a Belt
item.description:
Twice this week, men arrived at Miami International Airport from Havana and aroused the suspicions of customs officers for the same reason.

Something seemed to be concealed beneath their clothing.

The something, they found, turned out to be clutches of live birds hidden on their persons. In one of the arrests, 10 birds were stuffed in the man’s underpants, according to charging documents. The other man was smuggling 11 birds.

That man, Alberto Hernandez Castillo, disembarked from his flight on Sunday in a pair of gold-sheened sneakers, according to a criminal complaint. He appeared nervous and authorities observed an “unexplained bulge” around his pelvis.

The second man, Roberto Perez Quincosa, 41, who arrived on Tuesday, was also arrested after officials made similar observations about him.

Each man was charged with smuggling.

Authorities have not said if the cases were related. A lawyer for Mr. Hernandez Castillo did not respond to a request for comment. It was unknown if Mr. Perez Quincosa had a lawyer.

A pat-down found that Mr. Hernandez Castillo had black pouches sewn into his underpants, according to an account in the complaint from a special agent with Homeland Security Investigations. Nestled inside were six slim tubes, bound in beige tape and affixed with black mesh at the opening. Each contained one or two breathing birds, the complaint said.

Mr. Perez Quincosa had devised a belt-like garment to hold the 11 birds he carried, according to an account from a special agent with U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service that was included in a criminal complaint. He had used hair roller tubes “with holes along their length and capped with netting material,” wrapped in electrical tape, the complaint said.

Some of the birds that were recovered, such as the two blue grosbeaks that the authorities said Mr. Castillo had on him, are protected species. Eight yellow-faced grassquits were also found on him. Mr. Perez Quincosa had transported six Cuban melodious finches and five Cuban bullfinches, according to the complaint.

Yellow-faced grassquits are native to South and Central America and are named for the bands of yellow above the eyes and across the throats of males. Blue grosbeaks are North American songbirds.

Mr. Hernandez Castillo and Mr. Perez Quincosa were both born in Cuba and are now permanent U.S. residents, according to the complaints. Neither had filed the appropriate paperwork to legally import wildlife into the United States, and they had also checked “no” on customs declarations forms when asked if they were bringing animals or wildlife into the country.

Mr. Hernandez Castillo was released on Monday after posting a $25,000 bond, according to court records. The authorities did not say on Thursday if Mr. Perez Quincosa was still in custody.

Homeland Security Investigations and U.S. Customs and Border Protection referred inquiries to the Fish and Wildlife Service, which said in an email that it could not comment because it was still investigating.

The authorities did not say what happened to the birds, although trafficked animals sometimes are handed over to a zoo or shelter.

Miami is a gateway for smugglers seeking to bring wildlife into the United States from Latin America and the Caribbean, many of them to be offered for sale. The World Wildlife Fund estimates that, globally, as many as 1.5 million birds have been trafficked in a single year. Exotic birds with colorful plumage can sell for a thousand dollars or more. Global profits can reach the tens of billions of dollars, according to Bird Life International, a conservation group.

Last year, a man crossed from Mexico into California with two sedated parrots hidden in his trousers. In 2018, at least 200 finches made their way from South to North America stuffed in plastic hair rollers or in luggage. And six years before that, Interpol raids on airports, post offices pet stores and other settings in 32 countries uncovered more than 8,000 wild animals, most of them birds.

According to the complaints, Mr. Perez Quincosa told law enforcement that he knew bringing in the birds was unlawful and that he intended to breed and sell them for $100 to $120 each. Mr. Hernandez Castillo said that the birds he was carrying were intended for his “personal use,” according to the complaint. He then invoked his right to remain silent.

Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

item.title: Army Actions Contributed to Reagan Airport Collision, Internal Report Says
item.description:
Army investigators have concluded that problems with military training and helicopter technology contributed to a midair collision between an Army Black Hawk helicopter and a passenger jet that killed 67 people last year.

The internal report, copies of which were provided to reporters by relatives of crash victims Thursday, included recommendations to improve deficiencies that investigators said played a role in the January 2025 incident near Ronald Reagan National Airport, which is just outside of Washington. The episode prompted federal investigations and a national debate about aviation safety.

Like the National Transportation Safety Board, the independent federal agency that investigates aviation accidents, Army investigators found that the helicopter’s location-broadcasting technology had not been functioning properly on the night of the incident. They also concluded that officials had known that the helicopter’s altitude gauges could give faulty readings.

They recommended technology upgrades and urged that certain military aircraft be required to turn on location-broadcasting software while operating flights through the Washington area, “except when supporting an actual national security contingency.” They did not specify what constituted such an occurrence.

Safety advocates, lawmakers and the families of victims have been calling for stricter laws to prevent collisions between military aircraft and commercial flights around the busiest U.S. airports. Army investigators suggested in their report that the military was capable of self-regulating, and did not need new laws.

“Aircraft should be able to see each other in the sky,” Families of Flight 5342, a group formed among the relatives of those who died in the crash, said in a statement. “The technology is proven. All that’s required is the political will to do the right thing.”

The group added: “There is nothing left for Congress to wait for.”

The Army did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The pilots operating the Army Black Hawk involved in the collision were flying a national security training mission the night of the accident. Since then, the Federal Aviation Administration has changed the route the Army helicopter had been flying along near Reagan National and limited helicopter activity in the area to only critical emergency or military missions, such as transporting the president.

Lawmakers are currently debating whether such restrictions should be codified, as part of legislation to mandate the use of advanced technology.

The Army’s report agreed with N.T.S.B. recommendations urging leaders to create a database for reporting and analyzing incidents, to better understand the risks of flying through dense, complex airspace, and to offer more training to pilots operating flights in those areas.

But it differs from the N.T.S.B. on whether its own pilots might have erred on the night of the accident.

The N.T.S.B. determined that the helicopter pilots likely made a mistake when asking air traffic controllers at Reagan National for permission to fly through the area relying on their own ability to see and avoid obstacles. Army investigators, however, did not find evidence that the helicopter crew ignored any information.

Rather, they blamed the air traffic controller for insufficiently warning the pilots that they were on a collision course.

item.title: Fort Hood Shooter’s Execution Will be Public and Streamed Live, Pentagon Says
item.description:
Pentagon officials said on Thursday that the Army officer convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting would be executed in public, a practice that ended in the United States nearly a century ago and is most commonly carried out in a handful of countries including Iran, North Korea and the Taliban-led government in Afghanistan.

The Pentagon said in a statement that the military execution, scheduled for Dec. 3, would also be broadcast via livestream. Such a broadcast has little precedent, and releasing video of executions is most often associated with extremist militant groups like the Islamic State.

The announcement adds to the growing spectacle around the planned execution of Maj. Nidal Malik Hasan, who killed 13 people and wounded 32 others when he brought a personal handgun onto the grounds of Fort Hood, Texas. The rampage was the deadliest shooting at an American military base and sent shock waves through the U.S. military.

There are few countries that hold public executions. The human rights group Amnesty International has highlighted some cases in which public executions in Iran and Saudi Arabia have been filmed by bystanders.

The practice of filming and releasing video of an execution is more common with terror groups like the Islamic State, which became infamous for videos of gruesome executions of prisoners who were not given due process or convicted of crimes. Mass shooters have in some cases broadcast their killing sprees on livestream sites.

In an interview with Real America’s Voice, a conservative outlet, aboard the aircraft carrier U.S.S. Abraham Lincoln, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said Thursday that the execution would be public and available to watch “because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.” The Pentagon later confirmed in a statement that the execution would be livestreamed.

The Army has said the public execution of Major Hasan will be conducted by firing squad at Fort Hood, the site of the shooting. If carried out, it would be a first in modern American history.

The last state-sanctioned public execution in the United States occurred more than 90 years ago in Owensboro, Kentucky. Some 20,000 people gathered to witness the August 1936 hanging of Rainey Bethea, a young Black man who had been convicted of raping an elderly white woman.

Major Hasan’s execution would be the first by the military justice system since 1961, and he would be the first soldier put to death by firing squad since World War II. The firing squad is a rare method of execution, but one that has been used by the military, particularly during wartime. The Trump administration has proposed expanding its use as a method of execution.

Mr. Hegseth said that the decision to shoot Major Hasan by a firing squad, as well as other details of the execution, were chosen for their symbolism.

“Of course we’re going to do it at Fort Hood,” Mr. Hegseth said. “And do it on a Thursday and we’re going to do it at 1 o’clock — which is when he did it — and it’s going to be soldiers with rifles executing the firing squad. It hadn’t been since World War II since we’ve done that.”

He continued, “Well I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II.”

On Nov. 5, 2009, Major Hasan, an Army psychiatrist stationed at Fort Hood, brought a personal handgun onto the base grounds and opened fire. Major Hasan said that he carried out the attack, which occurred at the height of the post-9/11 fight against terrorism, to wage jihad for what he called the illegal and immoral wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. He admitted to the killings during his court-martial and was convicted in 2013 of 45 counts of premeditated murder and attempted premeditated murder.

Major Hasan, who was wounded in the shooting, is being held at the military death row prison in Fort Leavenworth, Kan. He expressed no remorse for his actions, and told a military mental health panel that he wished he had died in the attack so that he could have become a martyr.

Mr. Hegseth and other Pentagon officials emphasized Major Hasan’s motivations for the shooting in their public statements about the execution. Mr. Hegseth also criticized President Barack Obama for not describing the attack at the time as an act of terror.

Speaking at a rally in Texas on Wednesday, Mr. Trump, a vocal advocate of the death penalty, trumpeted his order to execute Major Hasan, telling the crowd in San Antonio that “we are going to deliver final justice to an evil killer.”

item.title: How Trump Has Alienated G.O.P. Voters
item.description:
I have been talking to working-class Americans about their political preferences since 2016, and have written many stories about how Donald Trump inspired them. Now, after 10 years, a war and sky-high fuel prices, more and more working-class Americans I am talking to are saying they’ve had enough.

Like Jim Pasek, 80, a retired pharma plant custodian, who loved Trump in the early years but now says, “He’s not making sense.” Or Sebastian Covey, 24, a landscaper, who cast a ballot for Trump in the first vote of his life and now is scrambling to find a carpool partner after swapping his truck for a car to cope with the rising cost of gas.

Many Americans still support Trump. But something is happening to his support that I have not seen since he took the political establishment by storm a decade ago.

One statistic from our public opinion poll last month that I find particularly relevant: Just 29 percent of likely Republican voters said the economy was better than it had been a year ago, down from 72 percent in January.

That sentiment is settling into this midterm election, dragging down Republican enthusiasm in a pattern that the independent political analyst Charlie Cook has termed the “red undertow.” Cook points out that it does not mean these disenchanted Republicans will vote for Democrats. Most will not. As Lindsay Kronemeyer, a 35-year-old Christian conservative, told me, “My belief system is still the same.” Instead, Cook argues, the dynamic will be a hindrance for Republican candidates, particularly in close races.

But Kronemeyer, an up-and-coming member of the Republican Party in Michigan who canvassed for Trump in 2016 and in 2020, wants to think about the party’s future. And Trump, she says, is not part of it. “He’s just not there in my head anymore,” she told me.

Debate Week

The main event last night was in Iowa, where Representative Ashley Hinson, the Republican candidate for Senate, and State Representative Josh Turek, her Democratic opponent, sparred “politely but sharply,” as Bayliss Wagner wrote.

A couple of Bayliss’s takeaways from the debate:

The Iran war, and its fallout, was a major issue. Hinson has voted against resolutions to rein in Trump’s war powers, and Turek sought to capitalize on it, telling voters, “When you’re struggling at the pump, that is because of Ashley Hinson.” Hinson tried to thread the needle between support for Trump and concern over the war, saying the conflict needed to come to “an immediate and successful end.”

Both candidates highlighted their bipartisanship. Turek, who was once a registered Republican, emphasized that he had voted hundreds of times with Republicans in the State House, while Hinson promoted her work with the Democratic former House speaker Nancy Pelosi.

The schedule picks up, with debates in Michigan, Maine and Georgia. They’ll offer a glimpse of three very different election landscapes: In Georgia, Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat, looks so solid that Republicans have pulled back on TV ads, while in Maine, the incumbent Republican, Senator Susan Collins, has been looking stronger in polls.

And in Michigan, the race between Dr. Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers appears to be neck and neck. We’ll be covering that one live. Follow along here.

Get Caught Up

Trump was in San Antonio last night to pump up Ken Paxton’s Senate campaign. But his speech seemed more focused on getting voters excited about Trump himself, writes Shawn McCreesh. (And, as usual, Trump insulted Paxton’s appearance.)

In the hours before the Michigan debate, Trump referred to El-Sayed as “Mohammed” in a Truth Social post. El-Sayed responded, “He knows my name is Abdul,” and said the president was trying to distract voters from his unpopular policies.

Trump will hold a rally in Alaska next week to boost the re-election campaigns of Senator Dan Sullivan and Representative Nick Begich, who are locked in competitive races.

The Michigan Corn Growers Association endorsed Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor. It’s the first time the group has endorsed a Democrat for governor, a spokeswoman said, another sign of how Republican policies on trade have scrambled the party’s agricultural base.

This Week in Polls

The Times’s poll tracker updates every day with new polls from around the country. Here are a few recent additions that caught the eye of Ruth Igielnik, an editor on our polling team.

A new CNN/SSRS poll in the Ohio Senate race shows the Democrat, Sherrod Brown, up by 6 percentage points over the incumbent Jon Husted. Three quarters of likely voters said Trump’s policies had increased the cost of living, and a majority were concerned about tariffs and gas prices.

In Iowa, the same poll found that voters are increasingly willing to split their ballots. Hinson, the Republican, has an edge in the Senate race, while Rob Sand, the Democrat, holds a 9-point lead in the governor’s race. (Our own Times/Siena poll last week suggested a similar dynamic at play.)

Polls in Florida, however, show a far less competitive Senate race. A Mason-Dixon poll found Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent, up 10 percentage points over Angie Nixon, which is consistent with what other recent polls have shown.

Meanwhile, views of Trump continue to sink. Only 17 percent of adults approve of his handling cost of living in the latest AP-NORC poll. And, more striking, only 38 percent of Republicans approve of him on the measure.

Where’s Jess?

I’m on the campus of Bethany College — which is affiliated with the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America — today for a Senate candidate’s campaign event. Can you guess what race I’m covering?

Alaska

Kansas

Maine

New Hampshire

Texas

Guess a state, and I’ll take you to the correct race’s polling page so you can see if you got it right. I’ll have more to say about my trip in an upcoming newsletter.

ONE LAST THING

As the temperature drops, Mainers are stressing. That’s because half the homes in Maine rely on oil for heat, and the war in Iran has caused prices to surge.

The issue is moving to the center of the Senate race. Troy Jackson, the Democratic candidate, brought it up at a town hall event this week, joking that people might have to get creative in heating their homes if they can’t shell out money for oil.

“It’s a good thing that Susan Collins got all those fire stations,” he said, referring to the pride his Republican opponent has expressed in her efforts to secure federal funds for fire stations. “Because we’re going to have a lot of fires.”

Some in the crowd laughed — though one person in the back muttered that Jackson’s line was not funny.

Taylor Robinson contributed to this newsletter.

item.title: ‘You’ve Hired Half the Third Reich’: 6 Key Moments From the Georgia Senate Debate
item.description:
Senator Jon Ossoff, the Democratic incumbent, and Representative Mike Collins, the Republican challenger, faced off Thursday night in the first debate in the battle for Georgia’s Senate seat.

The pressure was on Mr. Collins, who lags in the polls, to show that he is still in the fight to represent a state that President Trump carried in 2024. The two-term congressman’s polling numbers have looked so dismal that some Republicans have shifted resources away from the race.

Mr. Collins held his own against the more polished Mr. Ossoff on Thursday, but the zingers of the night came from the incumbent.

Here are six key moments from the debate in Georgia, where the election outcome on Nov. 3 could help determine control of the Senate.

Mr. Ossoff asked Mr. Collins at least eight times to explain how President Trump’s tariffs have helped Georgians. We counted.

The question was at the core of the incumbent’s strategy to hold Mr. Collins accountable for his voting record over the last year. In addition to tariffs, Mr. Ossoff returned time and again to Mr. Collins’s support for the war in Iran and his vote to pass Mr. Trump’s signature domestic policy bill, which included cuts to Medicaid and health insurance premiums.

Mr. Ossoff was clearly trying to portray Mr. Collins as nothing more than a yes man to Mr. Trump who has played a role in a second term that many Georgians are frustrated with.

“Whatever Donald Trump says," Mr. Ossoff said, “Mike Collins does.”

In many of the most heated moments of the debate, Mr. Collins returned to one of his favorite attacks against Mr. Ossoff: that he comes from a wealthy family.

Mr. Collins called Mr. Ossoff a “trust fund kid who’s never had a job in his life” and who does not care about gas prices because he “wants you riding on mass transit.”

Mr. Ossoff — whose primary holding is a blind trust worth between $1 million and $5 million, according to his financial disclosures — did not engage with the jabs for most of the debate. But in his closing argument, he returned fire at Mr. Collins for portraying himself as an everyday trucker when in reality he owns a trucking company worth as much as $25 million, according to his financial disclosure report.

In one of the zingers of the night, Mr. Ossoff accused Mr. Collins of hiring “half the Third Reich,” referring to the Republican congressman’s history of hiring aides who have espoused white nationalist and antisemitic views.

In another attack line that immediately circulated on social media, the Democrat also slammed Mr. Collins for reposting a video in 2024 of white male students taunting and jeering at a female Black student with racist and profane remarks.

“If John Lewis were marching today from Selma to Montgomery,” Mr. Ossoff said, “Mike Collins would be grabbing a billy club.”

Over the summer, a former intern and contractor for Mr. Collins’s leadership PAC posted a picture of himself on social media dressed in Ku Klux Klan robes, the Washington Post reported. Collins’s son-in-law has a track record of sharing Nazi imagery. And, according to a report in The Daily Beast on Thursday, two people who worked with his campaign were members of a group founded by a former member of the Klan.

A spokesman for Mr. Collins said the two people were unpaid volunteers, and the campaign did not know of their past associations.

Onstage, Mr. Collins did not directly deny the allegations. He said he has “condemned racism, antisemitism, hate.”

To confront one of the most charged issues of this election cycle, Mr. Collins brought up a Senate candidate hundreds of miles away from the one standing next to him: Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan.

Mr. Collins said that Mr. Ossoff supports Dr. El-Sayed, whom he characterized as a Democrat who “hates Israel” and “loves Iran.”

Asked whether Israel is “guilty of committing genocide” in Gaza, Mr. Ossoff said it’s a question for the International Criminal Court, and accused Mr. Collins of wanting to “sanction and defund” the court.

Mr. Ossoff, who is Jewish, also said that he “cares deeply” about the security of Israeli people, “some of whom are members of my family,” and about “innocent Palestinian life.”

Mr. Ossoff turned a question about whether the federal government should set voting rules into an attack on Mr. Collins and Mr. Trump for what he described as being “obsessed with overturning the 2020 election.”

The issue is resonant in Georgia, which became the focal point for election denial in 2020, when Mr. Trump called the Republican secretary of state and asked him to “find” enough votes to reverse Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s victory.

Mr. Collins countered by trying to tar Mr. Ossoff for opposing federal voter identification legislation, known as the SAVE America Act, which would impose stricter voter ID rules and require proof of citizenship to vote.

“People will go vote when they have confidence in our elections,” Mr. Collins said.

It was none other than Mr. Collins who brought up speculation about Mr. Ossoff’s ambitions.

He referred to the possibility that his opponent is considering a presidential run by saying that Hasan Piker, a provocative liberal streamer, had “endorsed Jon Ossoff for president for 2028.”

Mr. Piker has not, in fact, made an endorsement. And Mr. Ossoff has not declared any intentions … yet.

Taylor Robinson contributed reporting.

item.title: Arlington County Sues to Block Trump’s Triumphal Arch
item.description:
The county board in Arlington, Va., sued the Trump administration on Thursday to block the construction of President Trump’s proposed triumphal arch in Washington.

Arlington County is home to the Pentagon and Arlington National Cemetery, the hallowed military gravesite that is central to the legal battle over the planned arch. The Park Service has acknowledged that the arch, given its huge scale, would “adversely affect” the visual link between the cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial on the opposite side of the Potomac River, obstructing, for example, the view from President John F. Kennedy’s grave.

The five-member Arlington County Board is made up entirely of Democrats. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won the county in the 2024 presidential election with 78 percent of the vote.

In the lawsuit — directed at the National Park Service and Doug Burgum, the interior secretary — the county officials argued that the Trump administration failed to comply with a legally mandated review of the environmental impact of building the arch.

The officials said in the suit that they were seeking “to halt the agency’s feverish pace toward construction of the arch and to ensure that the ‘hard look’ mandated” by law “is completed before the agency commences disruptive and harmful ground-disturbing activities.”

The National Park Service has steamrolled through statutorily required reviews of the arch project, despite outside objections and its own assessment that the monument would alter views at dozens of historic sites near it.

The administration is planning for the arch to come before the National Capital Planning Commission for a final vote on Nov. 5, two days after the midterm elections.
